attributes.name: LiveLoggingSystem
attributes.description:
[LLM] The LiveLoggingSystem component utilizes a modular architecture, with separate components for logging, transcript processing, and configuration validation. This is evident in the directory structure, where the 'integrations' folder contains subfolders for 'browser-access', 'code-graph-rag', and 'copi', each representing a distinct aspect of the system. For instance, the 'copi' subfolder contains files such as 'INSTALL.md' and 'USAGE.md', which provide installation and usage guidelines for the Copi component. The 'lib/agent-api' folder contains the TranscriptAdapter abstract base class, which is responsible for reading and converting transcripts from different agent formats. The 'scripts' folder contains the LSLConfigValidator, which is used for validating and optimizing LSL configuration. The logging module, located in 'integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/logging.ts', provides a unified logging interface and is used throughout the system.

[LLM] The LiveLoggingSystem component employs the OntologyClassificationAgent, located in 'integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/ontology-classification-agent.ts', for classifying observations against an ontology system. This agent is used in conjunction with the logging module to provide a comprehensive logging experience. The OntologyClassificationAgent is responsible for categorizing observations into predefined categories, allowing for more efficient analysis and processing of logs. The 'integrations/mcp-constraint-monitor/docs/CLAUDE-CODE-HOOK-FORMAT.md' file provides documentation on the Claude Code Hook Data Format, which is used by the OntologyClassificationAgent. The 'lib/agent-api/transcripts/lsl-converter.js' file contains the LSLConverter, which is used for converting between agent-specific transcript formats and the unified LSL format.

[LLM] The LSLConfigValidator, located in 'scripts/validate-lsl-config.js', plays a crucial role in ensuring the validity and optimality of the LSL configuration. This script is responsible for parsing the LSL configuration file and checking for any errors or inconsistencies. The 'integrations/copi/INSTALL.md' file provides installation guidelines for the Copi component, which includes configuring the LSL settings. The 'integrations/copi/USAGE.md' file provides usage guidelines for the Copi component, which includes examples of how to use the LSL configuration. The 'lib/agent-api/transcript-api.js' file contains the TranscriptAdapter abstract base class, which is responsible for reading and converting transcripts from different agent formats.

[LLM] The logging module, located in 'integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/logging.ts', provides a unified logging interface and is used throughout the system. This module is responsible for handling log entries and providing a standardized way of logging events. The 'integrations/mcp-constraint-monitor/docs/constraint-configuration.md' file provides documentation on the Constraint Configuration Guide, which is used in conjunction with the logging module. The 'integrations/code-graph-rag/README.md' file provides an overview of the Graph-Code system, which is used for graph-based RAG analysis and is integrated with the LiveLoggingSystem component.

[LLM] The TranscriptAdapter abstract base class, located in 'lib/agent-api/transcript-api.js', provides a standardized way of reading and converting transcripts from different agent formats. This abstract base class is extended by concrete transcript adapter classes, such as the LSLConverter, which is located in 'lib/agent-api/transcripts/lsl-converter.js'. The 'integrations/copi/docs/hooks.md' file provides documentation on the Hook Functions Reference, which is used in conjunction with the TranscriptAdapter. The 'integrations/copi/scripts/README.md' file provides an overview of the Copi Tmux Status Line Integration, which is used in conjunction with the TranscriptAdapter.

[LLM] The LiveLoggingSystem component utilizes a variety of configuration files and environment variables to customize its behavior. For example, the 'integrations/copi/INSTALL.md' file provides installation guidelines for the Copi component, which includes configuring environment variables such as 'BROWSER_ACCESS_PORT' and 'BROWSER_ACCESS_SSE_URL'. The 'integrations/mcp-constraint-monitor/docs/constraint-configuration.md' file provides documentation on the Constraint Configuration Guide, which is used to configure the behavior of the LiveLoggingSystem component. The 'lib/agent-api/transcript-api.js' file contains the TranscriptAdapter abstract base class, which is responsible for reading and converting transcripts from different agent formats.

[LLM] The TranscriptAdapter abstract base class in `lib/agent-api/transcript-api.js` enforces a strict interface contract through explicit runtime errors rather than TypeScript abstract methods, meaning any subclass that fails to override `getAgentType()`, `getTranscriptDirectory()`, `readTranscripts()`, `convertToLSL()`, or `getCurrentSession()` will receive a thrown Error at call time. This pattern was likely chosen because parts of the codebase predate or coexist with plain JavaScript, making compile-time enforcement unavailable. The base class owns shared session caching via a `Map<sessionId, LSLSession>` instance, so all adapter subclasses inherit the same cache lifecycle — this means cache invalidation bugs in one agent's adapter could theoretically affect another if session ID namespacing is not carefully managed. The poll-based watch loop also lives in the base class, meaning the polling interval is uniform across all agent types (Claude Code JSONL, Copilot CLI, etc.) rather than being tunable per agent, which may cause unnecessary I/O for slow-moving transcript sources.

[LLM] LSLConverter in `lib/agent-api/transcripts/lsl-converter.js` uses a switch statement keyed on `LSLEntryType` enum values to dispatch between two rendering paths: Markdown (with `##` headers for user/assistant turns and `###` for tool calls) and JSON-Lines. The `options.includeToolResults` flag gates whether tool result entries are emitted at all, which means downstream consumers reading the JSONL output may see tool invocations without their results if this flag is false — a subtle asymmetry that could confuse replay or analysis tooling. The `maxContentLength` truncation is applied at the converter level rather than at capture time, so raw transcripts always preserve full fidelity and truncation is purely a rendering concern. Developers adding a new `LSLEntryType` must update the switch in LSLConverter or the entry will fall through silently, producing no output — there is no exhaustiveness check enforcing coverage of all enum variants.

[LLM] User identity anonymization in `scripts/validate-lsl-config.js` via `validateUserEnvironment()` computes a SHA-256 hash of the `USER` environment variable and takes the first 6 hex characters as the `userHash` written into `LSLMetadata`. This 6-character prefix provides only 16^6 = ~16.7 million distinct values, which is sufficient for separating a handful of developer identities but would produce collisions in large-scale deployments. The `multiUser.userHashLength` config field is validated to be between 6 and 12 characters, so operators can increase collision resistance up to 16^12 ≈ 281 trillion values, but the default of 6 is the floor. Critically, the hash is derived solely from the OS username with no salt, meaning the same user on two machines produces the same hash — this is by design for log correlation across hosts, but it also means the hash is deterministically reversible via rainbow table for common usernames like 'admin' or 'ubuntu'.

[LLM] The semantic analysis logging subsystem in `integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/logging.ts` uses an async write buffer capped at 50 entries with a 100ms flush interval, backed by `fsp.appendFile` to avoid blocking the Node.js event loop. This means log entries can be lost if the process crashes between flushes — the 100ms window represents a durability gap. The buffer cap of 50 entries acts as a backpressure mechanism: if the buffer fills before the flush interval fires, a flush is presumably triggered early, but if the flush itself is slow (e.g., disk I/O contention), entries may be dropped or the buffer may block. Log files are written to `$CODING_REPO/.data/logs/semantic-analysis-YYYY-MM-DD.log` with date-based rotation, but there is no apparent size-based rotation for these semantic analysis logs, unlike the main LSL config which enforces a 1MB–100MB `maxFileSize` constraint — meaning semantic analysis logs could grow unbounded on a busy day.

[LLM] The OntologyClassificationAgent in `integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/ontology-classification-agent.ts` supports three `classificationMethod` values — 'heuristic', 'llm', and 'hybrid' — and enforces a `minConfidence` threshold of 0.6 before attaching `OntologyMetadata` to an observation. The heuristic path is presumably fast and deterministic (pattern/keyword matching), while the LLM path adds latency and token cost tracked in the aggregated usage statistics. The hybrid mode likely runs heuristic first and escalates to LLM only when heuristic confidence falls below the threshold, though this escalation logic is internal to the agent. Because confidence scores below 0.6 result in no ontology metadata being attached, downstream consumers must treat the absence of `OntologyMetadata` as a valid state — they cannot assume all captured observations have been classified. This creates a two-tier observation corpus: classified entries with structured ontology tags and unclassified entries that only carry raw transcript content.

[LLM] Session time windowing is implemented across two separate components that must remain in sync: `LSLMetadata.timeWindow` (e.g., '0800-0900') carries the window label in the log output format, while `scripts/enhanced-transcript-monitor.js` owns the actual boundary logic by detecting prompt-set completion events and writing to the appropriate hourly transcript file. This separation means the windowing semantic is split between a data field definition (in the metadata schema) and a behavioral policy (in the monitor script), with no single authoritative source enforcing that the two agree. If `enhanced-transcript-monitor.js` changes its windowing granularity — for example, switching from hourly to 30-minute windows — the `timeWindow` string format in `LSLMetadata` would need to be updated separately, and any consumers pattern-matching on the 'HHMM-HHMM' format would silently misparse the new format. The `.specstory/history/logs/` directory structure presumably mirrors these time windows in its file naming, creating a three-way coupling between the monitor script, the metadata schema, and the filesystem layout.

[LLM] The `TranscriptAdapter` abstract base class in `lib/agent-api/transcript-api.js` enforces its interface contract through a `new.target` guard at construction time rather than relying on TypeScript-style compile-time checks, meaning any attempt to instantiate `TranscriptAdapter` directly at runtime throws immediately. The five abstract methods—`getAgentType()`, `getTranscriptDirectory()`, `readTranscripts()`, `convertToLSL()`, and `getCurrentSession()`—are declared as methods that throw `Error('Must implement ...')` when called on the base class, so subclasses that forget to override any single method will fail loudly at the first invocation rather than silently returning undefined. This pattern enables agent-specific implementations (e.g., a Claude Code JSONL adapter vs. a Copilot CLI adapter) to be swapped into the same pipeline without modifying any downstream consumer. The pipeline composition is entirely interface-driven: callers depend only on the five-method contract, meaning adding a new agent type requires only creating a new subclass and registering it, with zero changes to conversion, classification, or persistence logic.

[LLM] The `LSLConverter` class in `lib/agent-api/transcripts/lsl-converter.js` implements a dual-format serialization strategy that serves two distinct consumer needs simultaneously. `toMarkdown()` produces human-readable output with time-stamped section headers per entry type, suitable for developer review and audit trails, while `toJSONL()` emits one JSON object per line with a mandatory metadata-first-line convention that enables streaming parsers to identify session context before processing any entries. The companion `fromJSONL()` method round-trips this format by treating the first line specially as session metadata and subsequent lines as typed `LSLEntry` objects. Configurable content truncation and secret redaction are applied at serialization time rather than ingestion time, meaning the in-memory representation retains full fidelity while persisted forms are sanitized—this separation is critical for debugging (inspecting in-memory state) without risking credential leakage in log files. Tool result filtering is also applied during serialization, allowing verbose tool outputs to be stripped from the Markdown view while preserved in JSONL for downstream classifiers that need full tool context.

[LLM] The async buffered logging layer in `integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/logging.ts` solves a classic high-throughput I/O problem through two complementary mechanisms. A `logBuffer` string array accumulates log entries, and a `scheduleFlush()` function sets a 100ms timeout to batch-write them via `fsp.appendFile`. However, a hard ceiling of `MAX_BUFFER_SIZE = 50` entries triggers an immediate non-scheduled flush when the buffer fills, preventing unbounded memory growth during classification bursts. This dual-trigger design means normal operation benefits from batching (reducing syscall frequency) while pathological bursts are bounded. The use of `fsp.appendFile` (the promise-based `fs/promises` variant) rather than synchronous `fs.appendFileSync` is deliberate: synchronous writes would block the Node.js event loop during classification-heavy periods, degrading MCP server responsiveness. A new developer should note that this buffer is module-scoped, meaning it is shared across all log calls within a single MCP server process—there is no per-session or per-agent buffer isolation at this layer.

[LLM] The `LSLConfigValidator` in `scripts/validate-lsl-config.js` enforces explicit numeric bounds on every configurable LSL parameter rather than accepting any valid JavaScript number. For example, `fileManager.maxFileSize` is constrained between 1MB and 100MB, and `multiUser.userHashLength` between 6 and 12 characters. These bounds are not arbitrary: too-small file size limits cause excessive rotation churn that fragments session history across many files, while too-large limits create monolithic files that are slow to parse; similarly, hash lengths below 6 risk collision in multi-user environments while lengths above 12 waste filename space without security benefit. The validator also generates SHA-256 user hashes from the `USER` environment variable to provide multi-user session isolation without storing usernames directly in filenames—this is a privacy-preserving design choice that means log files are attributable only to users who know their own hash. Validation is run as a script rather than inline at runtime, suggesting it is intended as a CI gate or pre-deployment check rather than a hot-path guard.

[LLM] The two-tier log location strategy represents a deliberate separation between user-facing session history and system-level diagnostic logs. Session transcripts are standardized to `.specstory/history/logs/` (migrated from scattered per-project `logs/` directories), co-locating them with SpecStory history artifacts and making them discoverable through a single root regardless of which project is active. System and semantic analysis logs are routed to `CODING_REPO/.data/logs/` via the `setupLogging()` function in `integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/logging.ts`, keeping operational diagnostics separate from conversation history. This separation matters for tooling: the deduplication tooling that addressed 420 cross-project observation pollution incidents operates on `.specstory/history/logs/` entries, while monitoring and alerting tools target `CODING_REPO/.data/logs/`. The migration away from scattered per-project paths also means the health indicator `[LSL●]` in the tmux statusline (driven by `combined-status-line-wrapper.js`) can monitor a single canonical path rather than aggregating across variable project-specific locations.

[LLM] Session time-windowing, encoded as `timeWindow: '0800-0900'` in `LSLMetadata` (defined in both `transcript-api.js` and `lsl-converter.js`), introduces a clock-driven file routing mechanism that operates orthogonally to size-based rotation. Rather than only rotating when a file exceeds `maxFileSize`, the system can also route new entries to a new file when the clock crosses a window boundary, ensuring that each file corresponds to a bounded time period—useful for post-hoc analysis (e.g., 'what happened between 8am and 9am?') and for limiting the blast radius of a corrupt file to a one-hour window of sessions. The metadata-first-line convention in JSONL serialization means the `timeWindow` is always the first parseable field a streaming reader encounters, enabling fast file-level filtering without scanning entry bodies. A new developer extending the system should be aware that both `transcript-api.js` and `lsl-converter.js` define `LSLMetadata`—this duplication suggests the type was organically replicated rather than extracted to a shared types module, creating a risk of the two definitions diverging if one is updated without the other.

[LLM] The TranscriptAdapter abstract base class in `lib/agent-api/transcript-api.js` enforces a strict interface contract through explicit runtime errors rather than TypeScript abstract methods, meaning any subclass that fails to override `getAgentType()`, `getTranscriptDirectory()`, `readTranscripts()`, `convertToLSL()`, or `getCurrentSession()` will receive a thrown Error at call time. This pattern was likely chosen because parts of the codebase predate or coexist with plain JavaScript, making compile-time enforcement unavailable. The base class owns shared session caching via a `Map<sessionId, LSLSession>` instance, so all adapter subclasses inherit the same cache lifecycle — this means cache invalidation bugs in one agent's adapter could theoretically affect another if session ID namespacing is not carefully managed. The poll-based watch loop also lives in the base class, meaning the polling interval is uniform across all agent types (Claude Code JSONL, Copilot CLI, etc.) rather than being tunable per agent, which may cause unnecessary I/O for slow-moving transcript sources.

[LLM] LSLConverter in `lib/agent-api/transcripts/lsl-converter.js` uses a switch statement keyed on `LSLEntryType` enum values to dispatch between two rendering paths: Markdown (with `##` headers for user/assistant turns and `###` for tool calls) and JSON-Lines. The `options.includeToolResults` flag gates whether tool result entries are emitted at all, which means downstream consumers reading the JSONL output may see tool invocations without their results if this flag is false — a subtle asymmetry that could confuse replay or analysis tooling. The `maxContentLength` truncation is applied at the converter level rather than at capture time, so raw transcripts always preserve full fidelity and truncation is purely a rendering concern. Developers adding a new `LSLEntryType` must update the switch in LSLConverter or the entry will fall through silently, producing no output — there is no exhaustiveness check enforcing coverage of all enum variants.

This 6-character prefix provides only 16^6 = ~16.7 million distinct values, which is sufficient for separating a handful of developer identities but would produce collisions in large-scale deployments. The `multiUser.userHashLength` config field is validated to be between 6 and 12 characters, so operators can increase collision resistance up to 16^12 ≈ 281 trillion values, but the default of 6 is the floor. Critically, the hash is derived solely from the OS username with no salt, meaning the same user on two machines produces the same hash — this is by design for log correlation across hosts, but it also means the hash is deterministically reversible via rainbow table for common usernames like 'admin' or 'ubuntu'.

[LLM] The semantic analysis logging subsystem in `integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/logging.ts` uses an async write buffer capped at 50 entries with a 100ms flush interval, backed by `fsp.appendFile` to avoid blocking the Node.js event loop. This means log entries can be lost if the process crashes between flushes — the 100ms window represents a durability gap. The buffer cap of 50 entries acts as a backpressure mechanism: if the buffer fills before the flush interval fires, a flush is presumably triggered early, but if the flush itself is slow (e.g., disk I/O contention), entries may be dropped or the buffer may block. Log files are written to `$CODING_REPO/.data/logs/semantic-analysis-YYYY-MM-DD.log` with date-based rotation, but there is no apparent size-based rotation for these semantic analysis logs, unlike the main LSL config which enforces a 1MB–100MB `maxFileSize` constraint — meaning semantic analysis logs could grow unbounded on a busy day.

[LLM] The OntologyClassificationAgent in `integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/ontology-classification-agent.ts` supports three `classificationMethod` values — 'heuristic', 'llm', and 'hybrid' — and enforces a `minConfidence` threshold of 0.6 before attaching `OntologyMetadata` to an observation. The heuristic path is presumably fast and deterministic (pattern/keyword matching), while the LLM path adds latency and token cost tracked in the aggregated usage statistics. The hybrid mode likely runs heuristic first and escalates to LLM only when heuristic confidence falls below the threshold, though this escalation logic is internal to the agent. Because confidence scores below 0.6 result in no ontology metadata being attached, downstream consumers must treat the absence of `OntologyMetadata` as a valid state — they cannot assume all captured observations have been classified. This creates a two-tier observation corpus: classified entries with structured ontology tags and unclassified entries that only carry raw transcript content.

[LLM] Session time windowing is implemented across two separate components that must remain in sync: `LSLMetadata.timeWindow` (e.g., '0800-0900') carries the window label in the log output format, while `scripts/enhanced-transcript-monitor.js` owns the actual boundary logic by detecting prompt-set completion events and writing to the appropriate hourly transcript file. This separation means the windowing semantic is split between a data field definition (in the metadata schema) and a behavioral policy (in the monitor script), with no single authoritative source enforcing that the two agree. If `enhanced-transcript-monitor.js` changes its windowing granularity — for example, switching from hourly to 30-minute windows — the `timeWindow` string format in `LSLMetadata` would need to be updated separately, and any consumers pattern-matching on the 'HHMM-HHMM' format would silently misparse the new format. The `.specstory/history/logs/` directory structure presumably mirrors these time windows in its file naming, creating a three-way coupling between the monitor script, the metadata schema, and the filesystem layout.

[LLM] The `TranscriptAdapter` abstract base class in `lib/agent-api/transcript-api.js` enforces its interface contract through a `new.target` guard at construction time rather than relying on TypeScript-style compile-time checks, meaning any attempt to instantiate `TranscriptAdapter` directly at runtime throws immediately. The five abstract methods—`getAgentType()`, `getTranscriptDirectory()`, `readTranscripts()`, `convertToLSL()`, and `getCurrentSession()`—are declared as methods that throw `Error('Must implement ...')` when called on the base class, so subclasses that forget to override any single method will fail loudly at the first invocation rather than silently returning undefined. This pattern enables agent-specific implementations (e.g., a Claude Code JSONL adapter vs. a Copilot CLI adapter) to be swapped into the same pipeline without modifying any downstream consumer. The pipeline composition is entirely interface-driven: callers depend only on the five-method contract, meaning adding a new agent type requires only creating a new subclass and registering it, with zero changes to conversion, classification, or persistence logic.

[LLM] The `LSLConverter` class in `lib/agent-api/transcripts/lsl-converter.js` implements a dual-format serialization strategy that serves two distinct consumer needs simultaneously. `toMarkdown()` produces human-readable output with time-stamped section headers per entry type, suitable for developer review and audit trails, while `toJSONL()` emits one JSON object per line with a mandatory metadata-first-line convention that enables streaming parsers to identify session context before processing any entries. The companion `fromJSONL()` method round-trips this format by treating the first line specially as session metadata and subsequent lines as typed `LSLEntry` objects. Configurable content truncation and secret redaction are applied at serialization time rather than ingestion time, meaning the in-memory representation retains full fidelity while persisted forms are sanitized—this separation is critical for debugging (inspecting in-memory state) without risking credential leakage in log files. Tool result filtering is also applied during serialization, allowing verbose tool outputs to be stripped from the Markdown view while preserved in JSONL for downstream classifiers that need full tool context.

Rather than only rotating when a file exceeds `maxFileSize`, the system can also route new entries to a new file when the clock crosses a window boundary, ensuring that each file corresponds to a bounded time period—useful for post-hoc analysis (e.g., 'what happened between 8am and 9am?') and for limiting the blast radius of a corrupt file to a one-hour window of sessions. [LLM] The KnowledgeManagement component utilizes a GraphDatabaseAdapter for persistence, which is implemented in the file integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/storage/graph-database-adapter.ts. This adapter provides an interface for agents to interact with the central Graphology + LevelDB knowledge graph. The adapter also includes automatic JSON export sync, ensuring that the knowledge graph remains up-to-date. Furthermore, the migrateGraphDatabase script, located in scripts/migrate-graph-db-entity-types.js, is used to update entity types in the live LevelDB/Graphology database, demonstrating a clear focus on data consistency and integrity.

[LLM] The component follows a lock-free architecture, which is evident in the use of the VKB API when available and direct database access when the server is stopped. This design decision is reflected in the GraphDatabaseAdapter, where the VkbApiClient is used for VKB API interactions, with dynamic import to avoid TypeScript compilation issues. For example, in the file integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/storage/graph-database-adapter.ts, the VkbApiClient is imported dynamically using the require function, allowing for flexible and efficient API interactions.

[LLM] The KnowledgeManagement component employs a constructor-based pattern for agent initialization, as seen in the CodeGraphAgent and PersistenceAgent classes. The CodeGraphAgent, located in integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/code-graph-agent.ts, initializes the agent with a specific set of parameters, including the graph database adapter and the checkpoint manager. Similarly, the PersistenceAgent, located in integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/persistence-agent.ts, initializes the agent with a set of parameters, including the graph database adapter and the ontology system. This pattern allows for clear and concise agent initialization, making it easier for developers to understand and maintain the code.

[LLM] The component leverages a checkpoint system, managed by the CheckpointManager, to track analysis progress and entity updates. The CheckpointManager, located in integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/utils/checkpoint-manager.js, provides a clear and efficient way to manage checkpoints, ensuring that the knowledge graph remains up-to-date and consistent. For example, the CheckpointManager uses a JSON file to store checkpoint data, allowing for easy serialization and deserialization of checkpoint information. This design decision demonstrates a clear focus on data consistency and integrity, making it easier for developers to understand and maintain the code.

[LLM] The KnowledgeManagement component features UKB trace report generation, as implemented in the UKBTraceReport class. The UKBTraceReport, located in integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/utils/ukb-trace-report.ts, captures data flow and concept extraction details, providing valuable insights into the knowledge graph. The UKBTraceReport uses a combination of graph database queries and API interactions to generate the report, demonstrating a clear focus on data analysis and visualization. For example, the UKBTraceReport uses the GraphDatabaseAdapter to query the knowledge graph, and the VkbApiClient to interact with the VKB API, allowing for efficient and effective report generation.

[LLM] The component incorporates ontology classification, using the OntologySystem, to classify entities based on their types and properties. The OntologySystem, located in integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/ontology/index.js, provides a clear and efficient way to classify entities, ensuring that the knowledge graph remains consistent and up-to-date. For example, the OntologySystem uses a combination of graph database queries and API interactions to classify entities, demonstrating a clear focus on data analysis and visualization. The OntologySystem also uses a set of predefined ontologies, allowing for flexible and customizable entity classification.

[LLM] The KnowledgeManagement component implements a dual-mode storage architecture in GraphDatabaseAdapter (storage/graph-database-adapter.ts) that resolves the fundamental tension between LevelDB's single-writer constraint and a multi-process AI agent ecosystem. At initialization, the adapter calls VkbApiClient.isServerAvailable() and, depending on the result, configures itself to route all entity CRUD operations either through the VKB HTTP API (when the VKB server process is running) or directly through GraphDatabaseService (when the server is absent). This is not a runtime fallback — the mode is chosen once at startup and held for the adapter's lifetime, which means any consumer that initializes before the VKB server is ready will silently operate in direct-database mode for its entire lifecycle. The practical implication is that the VKB server must be started before any MCP server, agent, or script that wants lock-safe concurrent access; a race at startup degrades the multi-process safety guarantee to a single-process one without any error being raised. New developers should be aware that diagnosing LevelDB 'LOCK: Resource temporarily unavailable' errors requires checking whether the adapter initialized in direct mode rather than looking for obvious locking code elsewhere.

[LLM] PersistenceAgent (persistence-agent.ts) enforces a strict no-fallback rule at the point of entity persistence via GraphDatabaseAdapter.storeEntity(): if an entity's entityType field is missing or equals the string 'Unclassified', the method throws an explicit error annotated with the comment 'NO FALLBACKS'. This design reflects a hard-won lesson captured across several working-memory entries — earlier versions of the pipeline allowed entities to fall through with placeholder types, which caused the ontology classification step to silently re-run expensive LLM calls during persistence, adding roughly 200 seconds to wave-analysis workflow runs (see the memory note: 'entityType/type disconnect in coordinator ontology classification, line ~3098'). The enforcement is complemented upstream by a classificationCache (Map<string, ClassificationCacheEntry>) inside PersistenceAgent with a 5-minute TTL (CLASSIFICATION_CACHE_TTL_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000). Within a single workflow run, any entity name that was already classified within the TTL window is served from cache, bypassing the LLM entirely. This two-layer defense — cache-before-LLM plus hard error at persistence — forms the classification correctness contract for the whole knowledge pipeline.

[LLM] The SharedMemoryEntity schema defined in persistence-agent.ts is a deliberately rich structure that goes well beyond a simple key-value store. It carries bi-temporal staleness fields (staleness_score ranging 0–100, invalidating_commits as a string array, staleness_check_at as a timestamp, and staleness_method describing how staleness was computed), mirroring design patterns from the Graphiti temporal knowledge graph library. It also carries mixed_topics detection metadata: a boolean flag and an array of Jaccard-similarity pairs identifying which topic clusters share unexpectedly high lexical overlap, flagging entities whose content scope may have drifted too broad. Hierarchy is encoded as an integer level field (0 = Project, 1 = Component, 2 = SubComponent, 3 = Detail) rather than a string, so graph traversal code can use numeric comparisons instead of string matching. Finally, entities optionally carry a 384-dimensional dense embedding vector produced by the embedding operator, enabling future semantic similarity search without a separate vector index. Taken together, the schema design treats each entity not just as a knowledge record but as a versioned, spatially-located, topically-bounded artifact — a reflection of the project's ambition to support incremental, auditable knowledge evolution over git history.

[LLM] JSON export synchronization is handled through an event-driven side-channel rather than an explicit export call in the write path. After GraphDatabaseAdapter initializes in direct mode, it dynamically imports GraphKnowledgeExporter and attaches it to the GraphDatabaseService event bus, listening for 'entity:stored' events. When any entity is written, the event fires and GraphKnowledgeExporter incrementally updates the JSON export files at .data/knowledge-export/ without any caller in the write path needing to know the export exists. The dynamic import is a deliberate design choice: it avoids a hard circular dependency between the adapter and the exporter, and it means the exporter can fail to attach (logged as a warning) without aborting the write. The downside is that the export is only live in direct-database mode; in VKB-API mode, the HTTP server is responsible for triggering its own export events, and if that path diverges the JSON exports can become stale. Developers reading the codebase for the first time often miss that .data/knowledge-export/coding.json is not written by a scheduled job or a CLI command but is a continuous side-effect of every successful entity persistence event.

[LLM] The migrate-graph-db-entity-types.js migration script reveals how the KnowledgeManagement system handles schema evolution in a graph that has no migrations framework. The script iterates all nodes using Graphology's graph.forEachNode() callback API, rewrites legacy entity type strings (TransferablePattern, WorkflowPattern, TechnicalIssue, and others) to three canonical types (System, Project, Pattern) by calling graph.setNodeAttribute() in-place, then at the end sets isDirty = true on the GraphDatabaseService instance and calls dbService._persistGraphToLevel() directly — bypassing the normal entity-write path entirely. This approach works because Graphology is an in-memory graph and LevelDB is written in a single batch flush, making the migration atomic at the storage level. The risk is that the migration script accesses private API (_persistGraphToLevel) and assumes the internal isDirty flag exists and behaves as expected; any refactor that renames or removes that flag will silently break future migrations. The broader pattern — in-place attribute mutation followed by a manual dirty-flush — is the established idiom for one-shot schema migrations in this project, and new developers writing similar scripts should follow it rather than attempting to delete and re-insert nodes, which would break all relational edges.

[LLM] UKBTraceReportGenerator (utils/ukb-trace-report.ts) provides a structured audit trail for the wave-analysis workflow by recording DataLossTracking objects at each major pipeline stage: git history ingestion, vibe history ingestion, semantic analysis, and ontology classification. Each DataLossTracking record holds inputCount, outputCount, a computed lossPercentage, and a lossReasons string array describing why specific entities were filtered or dropped. The generator aggregates these per-batch records into a per-workflow summary that is emitted at the end of a run, allowing post-mortem inspection of exactly where in the pipeline entities vanished — a direct response to the earlier diagnosis bug where 'summary stats were broken (totalCommits:0, totalObservations:0) despite batches processing data' (working memory). The trace report is the primary tool for distinguishing between a healthy run that produced few entities because the codebase had few changes and a broken run that silently dropped entities mid-pipeline. Its existence also imposes an implicit discipline on pipeline authors: any new stage that filters or transforms entities is expected to register its loss accounting with the generator, making loss tracking an opt-in contract rather than a passive measurement.

The KnowledgeManagement component is the persistence and lifecycle layer for the project's knowledge graph, managing entity storage, retrieval, ontology classification, and knowledge decay using Graphology (in-memory directed graph) backed by LevelDB for durable persistence. The architecture is layered: GraphDatabaseService owns the raw graph and LevelDB I/O, GraphDatabaseAdapter wraps it with lock-free dual-mode routing (VKB HTTP API when the server is running, direct LevelDB access when stopped), and PersistenceAgent sits at the top as a workflow-facing orchestrator that enforces classification, deduplicates fuzzy name matches, and manages the bi-temporal staleness lifecycle. A parallel JSON export pipeline (GraphKnowledgeExporter) is dynamically attached at adapter initialization time so that every entity:stored event also updates the flat-file exports consumed by downstream tools.

Entities follow a four-level hierarchy (Project → Component → SubComponent → Detail) encoded directly in the SharedMemoryEntity schema via hierarchyLevel, parentEntityName, and childEntityNames fields. Classification is ontology-driven with a per-run LRU cache (5-minute TTL) to avoid redundant LLM calls, and unclassified entities are refused at the store boundary — GraphDatabaseAdapter.storeEntity() throws hard rather than silently writing an Unclassified node. Staleness is tracked bi-temporally: each entity carries invalidating_commits[], staleness_score (0–100), and staleness_check_at fields so git-commit-driven freshness assessment can surface stale nodes in the VKB viewer without a full re-analysis pass.

The component also includes a trace-reporting subsystem (ukb-trace-report.ts) that instruments every UKB workflow run with per-batch DataLossTracking structs, ontology classification audit trails, and observation derivation provenance. Migration scripts (scripts/migrate-graph-db-entity-types.js) operate directly on the live LevelDB graph via GraphDatabaseService, iterating nodes and rewriting entityType attributes before a manual persist call, providing a safe path for schema consolidation without taking the service offline.

GraphDatabaseAdapter (storage/graph-database-adapter.ts) implements lock-free dual-mode routing: it calls VkbApiClient.isServerAvailable() at initialization and routes all reads/writes through the VKB HTTP API when the server is up, switching to direct GraphDatabaseService access only when stopped — preventing LevelDB exclusive-lock conflicts between the VKB server and MCP agents.

PersistenceAgent (persistence-agent.ts) enforces a hard no-fallback classification contract: GraphDatabaseAdapter.storeEntity() throws 'Cannot store entity: entityType is Unclassified. NO FALLBACKS.' rather than silently writing unclassified nodes, ensuring ontology integrity at the persistence boundary.

EntityMetadata in SharedMemoryEntity (persistence-agent.ts) carries three bi-temporal staleness fields — invalidating_commits[] (git SHAs that may have made the entity stale), staleness_score (0–100), and staleness_check_at (ISO timestamp) — enabling git-commit-driven freshness assessment without a full re-analysis pass.

GraphDatabaseAdapter.initialize() (storage/graph-database-adapter.ts:160–175) dynamically imports GraphKnowledgeExporter from the repo root and attaches it to the live GraphDatabaseService instance so that entity:stored events trigger debounced JSON exports to .data/knowledge-export/; without this attachment the export files silently go stale.

PersistenceAgent uses a Map<string, ClassificationCacheEntry> with CLASSIFICATION_CACHE_TTL_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000 (persistence-agent.ts) to skip redundant LLM classification calls within a single workflow run, storing entityType, confidence, method, and ontologyMetadata per cache entry.

SharedMemoryEntity schema (persistence-agent.ts) encodes the four-level hierarchy directly in the entity record via hierarchyLevel (0=Project … 3=Detail), parentEntityName, childEntityNames[], and an isScaffoldNode boolean flag that marks L0–L2 structural nodes created by migration rather than organic analysis.

UKBTraceReport (utils/ukb-trace-report.ts) captures per-batch DataLossTracking structs with inputCount, outputCount, lossCount, lossPercentage, and lossReasons[] for every pipeline step, providing a full audit trail of where concepts are filtered or dropped across git-history, vibe-history, ontology-classification, and persistence stages.

Finally, entities optionally carry a 384-dimensional dense embedding vector produced by the embedding operator, enabling future semantic similarity search without a separate vector index. CodingPatterns serves as the architectural catch-all component for the Coding project, capturing cross-cutting programming conventions, design idioms, and best practices that pervade the codebase. The project demonstrates several recurring patterns: retry-with-backoff for service connections, mapping-based format conversion, DAG-based topological execution ordering, and lazy initialization for LLM clients. These patterns appear across integrations, scripts, and service layers rather than being isolated to a single module.

ConnectionManager uses retry-with-backoff in connectViaHTTP to establish resilient connections to services like the observations API (localhost:12436), making this the standard pattern for all inter-service HTTP communication in the project.

DAG-based execution ordering via topological sort is used in batch-analysis.yaml steps, establishing a declarative dependency-driven execution model for multi-step analysis workflows.

LSLConverter (src/live-logging/) uses a mapping-based approach to convert between transcript formats as defined in config/transcript-formats.json, centralizing format definitions outside code.

A two-commit pattern is enforced for knowledge exports: observation JSON and knowledge graph JSON are committed separately by artifact type, as documented in project conventions.

Services follow a fixed port registry convention documented in project knowledge: constraint-dashboard on 3030, obs_api on 12436, OKB retrieval/injection on 3848 — making port allocation explicit and collision-free.

UKBTraceReportGenerator delegates to CodeGraphAgent.generateReport() (integrations/mcp-server-src/) rather than implementing report logic directly, following a delegation pattern for graph-backed reporting.

PlantUML diagrams follow a project style guide enforcing kebab-case filenames and standard style file includes, with diagram sources stored alongside docs/images/ output artifacts.

CodingPatterns serves as the catch-all component for general programming wisdom, design patterns, and coding conventions observed across the Coding project. It encompasses architectural idioms that recur throughout the codebase, such as the graph-based persistence pattern using Graphology+LevelDB, the provider-agnostic abstraction pattern for LLMs, and the phase-based GSD planning workflow. attributes.name: ConstraintSystem
attributes.description:
[LLM] The ConstraintSystem component utilizes a GraphDatabaseAdapter for persistence, which is implemented in the storage/graph-database-adapter.ts file. This adapter enables the system to store and retrieve graph structures using Graphology and LevelDB, with automatic JSON export sync. The use of Graphology allows for efficient graph operations, while LevelDB provides a robust and scalable storage solution. The GraphDatabaseAdapter class in storage/graph-database-adapter.ts is responsible for managing the graph database, including creating and deleting graphs, as well as handling graph queries. The automatic JSON export sync feature ensures that the graph data is consistently updated and available for other components to access.

[LLM] The ContentValidationAgent, implemented in integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/content-validation-agent.ts, plays a crucial role in the ConstraintSystem component. This agent is responsible for checking entity content for accuracy and consistency, ensuring that the data stored in the graph database is valid and reliable. The ContentValidationAgent uses a combination of semantic analysis and machine learning algorithms to validate the content, and it provides refresh reports to the system. The agent's functionality is critical to the overall integrity of the ConstraintSystem, as it helps to prevent errors and inconsistencies in the data. The ContentValidationAgent class in content-validation-agent.ts includes methods for validating entity content, such as the validateEntityContent method, which takes an entity object as input and returns a validation result.

[LLM] The UnifiedHookManager, implemented in lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-manager.js, is a key component of the ConstraintSystem's hook management mechanism. This manager is responsible for loading and dispatching hook events to registered handlers, allowing the system to respond to various events and actions. The UnifiedHookManager uses a HookConfigLoader, implemented in lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-config.js, to load and merge hook configurations from multiple sources. The HookConfigLoader class in hook-config.js includes methods for loading hook configurations, such as the loadHookConfig method, which takes a configuration file path as input and returns a hook configuration object. The UnifiedHookManager then uses this configuration to dispatch hook events to the registered handlers.

[LLM] The ConstraintSystem component employs a ViolationCaptureService, implemented in scripts/violation-capture-service.js, to bridge live session logging with constraint monitor dashboard persistence. This service is responsible for capturing and storing violations that occur during live sessions, allowing the system to track and analyze errors and inconsistencies. The ViolationCaptureService uses the graph database to store the violations, ensuring that the data is persisted and available for later analysis. The service also provides a way to retrieve and display the violations in the constraint monitor dashboard, allowing developers to identify and address issues. The ViolationCaptureService class in violation-capture-service.js includes methods for capturing and storing violations, such as the captureViolation method, which takes a violation object as input and stores it in the graph database.

[LLM] The useWorkflowDefinitions hook, implemented in integrations/system-health-dashboard/src/components/workflow/hooks.ts, is used by the ConstraintSystem component to get workflow definitions from Redux. This hook allows the system to access and utilize workflow definitions, which are stored in the Redux state. The useWorkflowDefinitions hook returns a workflow definitions object, which includes information about the workflows, such as their names, descriptions, and steps. The system can then use this information to display and manage the workflows in the constraint monitor dashboard. The useWorkflowDefinitions hook is an example of how the ConstraintSystem component integrates with other components and systems, such as the system health dashboard, to provide a comprehensive and integrated experience.

[LLM] The ConstraintSystem component also employs a useNodeWiggle hook, implemented in integrations/system-health-dashboard/src/components/workflow/hooks.ts, for node wiggle animation. This hook allows the system to animate the nodes in the workflow graph, providing a visual representation of the workflow and its components. The useNodeWiggle hook takes a node object as input and returns an animation object, which includes information about the animation, such as its duration and timing. The system can then use this animation object to animate the node, creating a dynamic and engaging visual representation of the workflow. The useNodeWiggle hook is an example of how the ConstraintSystem component uses animation and visualization to enhance the user experience and provide a more engaging and interactive interface.

[LLM] The ConstraintSystem uses a dual-path persistence strategy in `scripts/violation-capture-service.js` that separates concerns between live consumption and historical querying. Every violation is written simultaneously to a streaming JSONL file at `.mcp-sync/session-violations.jsonl` (one record per line, suitable for `tail -f` or SSE-style push) and to a capped JSON history at `.mcp-sync/violation-history.json` that retains at most 1000 entries. This cap is a deliberate defense against unbounded disk growth across long sessions, but it introduces a subtle asymmetry: the JSONL log is an append-only stream with no cap, while the JSON history silently evicts older entries once the limit is reached. A new developer debugging why the dashboard shows fewer historical violations than the raw JSONL contains should look at this 1000-entry cap in `ViolationCaptureService`. The in-memory violations array serves as the authoritative source for `calculateStatistics()`, which computes a 24-hour rolling window count, per-severity breakdown, the most-frequently-fired constraint ID, and average violations per session — all derived without a separate aggregation store, meaning a process restart resets those running statistics even though the JSONL log survives on disk.

[LLM] Hook configuration is loaded through a strict two-layer merge in `HookConfigLoader` (`lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-config.js`). The user-level baseline at `~/.coding-tools/hooks.json` is read first, establishing defaults applicable across all projects, then the project-level file at `.coding/hooks.json` applies targeted overrides. Both layers are validated against a shared schema that requires `type` and `path` on every handler entry and enforces that `timeout` must be a positive number — meaning a project config that omits `timeout` entirely is valid (inheriting the user-level value), but one that sets `timeout: 0` or `timeout: -1` is rejected at load time. The `UnifiedHookManager` (`lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-manager.js`) then maintains a `Map<string, HookHandler[]>` keyed by `HookEvent` enum values imported from `hooks-api.js`. Each array is re-sorted by priority on every `registerHandler()` call, and duplicate handler IDs cause in-place replacement rather than accumulation. This means a second call to `registerHandler()` with the same ID is effectively an upsert — a safe default for reload scenarios, but developers extending the system should be aware that handler registration is idempotent by ID, not by position.

[LLM] Agent-scoped constraint enforcement is implemented via an `agents: string[]` field on each `HookHandler` in `UnifiedHookManager` (`lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-manager.js`). When the array is empty, the constraint fires for all agents (Claude Code, OpenCode, Copilot, Mastra); when non-empty, the manager filters handlers at dispatch time to only those whose `agents` list includes the currently active agent. This design allows a single `.coding/hooks.json` to express rules like 'enforce `no-console-log` only in Claude Code sessions' or 'apply the stricter TypeScript constraint only when Mastra is the executor' without requiring separate config files per agent. The practical implication is that a constraint violation seen in one agent session may not appear at all in another, which can create confusing discrepancies when comparing session violation histories. The `no-console-log` constraint documented in project memory as applying to Edit/Write on `.js/.ts` files is an example of a constraint that could have agent scope applied, though the current configuration appears to leave `agents: []` (all agents) for that rule based on the documented behavior that it fires consistently regardless of which agent is running.

[LLM] The `update_constraints` MCP tool exposes a live mutation surface that allows constraint rules — their `id`, `pattern`, `message`, `severity`, and `enabled` flag — to be patched at runtime inside a running Claude Code session without restarting the MCP server. This is a sharp double-edged capability: it supports rapid iteration when tuning a regex pattern that produces false positives, but it also means the effective ruleset during a session can diverge from whatever is committed in the config files. A developer who patches a rule via `update_constraints` mid-session to suppress a false positive must remember to also update the persistent config, or the next session will re-enable the original rule. There is no auditing trail for in-session mutations visible in the violation history — the `violation-history.json` records fired violations, not configuration change events. A future hardening improvement would be to emit a synthetic 'config mutation' event into the JSONL stream whenever `update_constraints` is invoked, providing a full audit log that pairs rule changes with the violations (or absence of violations) that followed.

[LLM] The `ContentValidationAgent` (`integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/content-validation-agent.ts`) represents a second validation tier that is architecturally distinct from the real-time MCP constraint checks but shares the same rule-and-report output model. Where the constraint monitor fires on individual tool calls within a Claude Code session, the `ContentValidationAgent` operates asynchronously on the UKB pipeline, using `GitStalenessDetector` to identify knowledge graph entities whose referenced file paths, CLI commands, or API endpoints no longer exist in the repository. It caches git commit data in `cachedGitCommits` with a 60-second TTL (`GIT_CACHE_TTL_MS = 60000`) to avoid redundant subprocess spawns during batch validation waves where many entities share the same recent commits. The 60-second TTL is a pragmatic balance: short enough to notice a commit made mid-wave, long enough to avoid git invocations becoming a bottleneck. A developer implementing a new type of staleness check should add it to `ContentValidationAgent` rather than the constraint monitor, since it targets knowledge graph integrity rather than session-time code quality. The two systems share the constraint ID/severity/message vocabulary but operate on completely different data sources and at different points in the development lifecycle.

[LLM] The `ViolationCaptureService.calculateStatistics()` method (`scripts/violation-capture-service.js`) computes all aggregates — 24-hour rolling window count, per-severity breakdown, most-frequently-fired constraint ID, and average violations per session — entirely from the in-memory violations array, with no separate aggregation store or database. This architectural choice keeps the statistics component stateless and restart-safe in the sense that there is no corruption risk from a partial write, but it makes the statistics inherently ephemeral: a process restart drops all in-memory state even though the `.mcp-sync/violation-history.json` persists on disk. After a restart, the service must re-hydrate its in-memory array by re-reading the JSON history file, but it will only see up to the 1000-entry cap — any violations evicted from the cap before the restart are permanently invisible to future statistics calculations. This means that sessions with extremely high violation rates (e.g., running a mass refactor that triggers `no-console-log` hundreds of times) can silently distort the average-violations-per-session metric by pushing older, quieter sessions out of the 1000-entry window. Developers interpreting dashboard trend data should treat the rolling statistics as a sliding window over recent activity rather than a true historical aggregate.

[LLM] The constraint monitor's integration with Claude Code operates at the MCP boundary rather than at the shell or filesystem level, which has a significant architectural consequence: constraints are only enforced when Claude Code is the active agent and has loaded the `mcp-constraint-monitor` server. This is by design for session-scoped enforcement, but it means that direct filesystem edits made outside a Claude Code session — by a human developer, a CI script, or another agent not configured to load the MCP server — bypass the constraint checks entirely. The hook infrastructure in `lib/agent-api/hooks/` mitigates this partially through the `HookEvent` pre-tool and post-tool events, which fire on every tool call that passes through `UnifiedHookManager`, but these hooks are still session-scoped. The system therefore provides strong enforcement during AI-assisted development sessions while leaving a gap for non-session edits. The project memory note that 'constraint violations = real issues' and 'NEVER work around constraint violations' is a process control compensating for this architectural gap — it relies on developer discipline during sessions to catch the violations that CI or pre-commit hooks would normally surface in a traditional enforcement pipeline.

[LLM] The ConstraintSystem uses a dual-file persistence strategy in ViolationCaptureService (scripts/violation-capture-service.js) that separates concerns between real-time streaming and historical analysis. Violations are written to .mcp-sync/session-violations.jsonl in newline-delimited JSON format, where each line is an independent JSON record — this format allows tail-based log streaming and incremental reads without parsing the entire file. Simultaneously, .mcp-sync/violation-history.json maintains a structured JSON array capped at 1000 entries, optimized for dashboard rendering that needs random access and aggregate statistics. The cap is enforced on every write by slicing the array to the last 1000 entries, meaning oldest violations are silently dropped. A new developer should be aware that these two files can diverge: the JSONL file is append-only and grows unbounded within a session, while the history file reflects only the most recent 1000 violations across all sessions. This design tradeoff prioritizes dashboard performance over complete audit history.

[LLM] The hook pipeline in lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-manager.js implements a priority queue pattern using a Map keyed by event type (pre-tool, post-tool as defined in the HookEvent enum in hooks-api.js), where each key maps to a sorted array of HookHandler objects. Lower numeric priority values execute earlier, meaning a constraint handler registered at priority 10 will fire before one at priority 100 for the same event. The sort is applied at registration time rather than execution time, which is an optimization that keeps the hot path (per-tool-call execution) free of sorting overhead at the cost of requiring re-sort if handlers are dynamically added after initialization. This architecture means constraint checks can be layered — for example, a fast syntactic check at priority 10 could short-circuit before an expensive semantic check at priority 50 — though whether such layering is currently exploited depends on the specific constraint handler registrations in the project's hooks configuration files.

[LLM] HookConfigLoader (lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-config.js) implements a two-level configuration merge where project-level settings (.coding/hooks.json) override user-level settings (~/.coding-tools/hooks.json). This follows the same layered pattern seen in many developer tools (e.g., ESLint, Git). The merge is not a deep recursive merge of individual handler properties — rather, project config takes precedence at the handler level, meaning a project can completely replace a user-defined handler for the same hook event. The validateConfig() method enforces that each handler has a required 'type' and 'path' field, that 'priority' is a number if present, and that 'agents' is an array if present. Crucially, validation failures emit warnings rather than throwing errors, so a misconfigured handler is silently skipped while valid handlers in the same config file continue to load. New developers adding custom constraint hooks should test their JSON structure carefully, as a typo in the config file will cause the hook to be silently ignored rather than producing a startup error.

[LLM] The agent-scoped filtering mechanism on HookHandler objects (the agents[] array field, processed in lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-manager.js) enables the ConstraintSystem to apply different enforcement rules to different AI coding agents running within the same infrastructure. When a tool call event fires, the UnifiedHookManager checks whether the triggering agent's identifier matches any entry in the handler's agents array before invoking the handler. If the agents array is absent or empty, the handler fires for all agents globally. This design is significant in multi-agent deployments (e.g., where both Claude and GitHub Copilot sessions may be active) because it prevents constraint rules tuned for one agent's tool-call patterns from producing false positives against another agent's different tool vocabulary. [LLM] The hook pipeline in lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-manager.js implements a priority queue pattern using a Map keyed by event type (pre-tool, post-tool as defined in the HookEvent enum in hooks-api.js), where each key maps to a sorted array of HookHandler objects. Lower numeric priority values execute earlier, meaning a constraint handler registered at priority 10 will fire before one at priority 100 for the same event. The sort is applied at registration time rather than execution time, which is an optimization that keeps the hot path (per-tool-call execution) free of sorting overhead at the cost of requiring re-sort if handlers are dynamically added after initialization. This architecture means constraint checks can be layered — for example, a fast syntactic check at priority 10 could short-circuit before an expensive semantic check at priority 50 — though whether such layering is currently exploited depends on the specific constraint handler registrations in the project's hooks configuration files.

[LLM] HookConfigLoader (lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-config.js) implements a two-level configuration merge where project-level settings (.coding/hooks.json) override user-level settings (~/.coding-tools/hooks.json). This follows the same layered pattern seen in many developer tools (e.g., ESLint, Git). The merge is not a deep recursive merge of individual handler properties — rather, project config takes precedence at the handler level, meaning a project can completely replace a user-defined handler for the same hook event. The validateConfig() method enforces that each handler has a required 'type' and 'path' field, that 'priority' is a number if present, and that 'agents' is an array if present. Crucially, validation failures emit warnings rather than throwing errors, so a misconfigured handler is silently skipped while valid handlers in the same config file continue to load. New developers adding custom constraint hooks should test their JSON structure carefully, as a typo in the config file will cause the hook to be silently ignored rather than producing a startup error.

[LLM] The agent-scoped filtering mechanism on HookHandler objects (the agents[] array field, processed in lib/agent-api/hooks/hook-manager.js) enables the ConstraintSystem to apply different enforcement rules to different AI coding agents running within the same infrastructure. When a tool call event fires, the UnifiedHookManager checks whether the triggering agent's identifier matches any entry in the handler's agents array before invoking the handler. If the agents array is absent or empty, the handler fires for all agents globally. This design is significant in multi-agent deployments (e.g., where both Claude and GitHub Copilot sessions may be active) because it prevents constraint rules tuned for one agent's tool-call patterns from producing false positives against another agent's different tool vocabulary. In practice, this means constraint configuration authors must be explicit about agent scope when writing handlers — an omitted agents field is a global match, which may be unintentionally broad.

[LLM] ViolationCaptureService.sanitizeParams() implements a security boundary between live session tool data and persisted violation records by redacting parameter values whose keys match a case-insensitive substring check against the set {'password', 'token', 'key', 'secret', 'auth'}. The redaction replaces the value with a placeholder string rather than removing the key entirely, preserving the structural shape of the parameter object for debugging while eliminating sensitive content. This is a defense-in-depth measure: even if violation log files are accidentally committed to version control or exposed via the dashboard API, credentials embedded in tool parameters (e.g., a Write tool call with an API key in the content) will not be leaked. However, the substring matching approach has both false positive risk (a parameter named 'monkey' would not match, but 'apikey' would due to containing 'key') and false negative risk (a sensitive parameter named 'credential' or 'bearer' would not be redacted). attributes.name: SemanticAnalysis
attributes.description:
[LLM] The SemanticAnalysis component employs a multi-agent architecture, utilizing agents such as the OntologyClassificationAgent, SemanticAnalysisAgent, and CodeGraphAgent, to perform tasks such as code analysis, ontology classification, and insight generation. The OntologyClassificationAgent, for instance, is implemented in the file integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/ontology-classification-agent.ts and is responsible for classifying observations against the ontology system. This agent-based approach allows for a modular and scalable design, enabling the component to handle large-scale codebases and provide meaningful insights.

[LLM] The component leverages the GraphDatabaseAdapter, implemented in the file storage/graph-database-adapter.js, for Graphology+LevelDB persistence with automatic JSON export sync. This adapter provides a standardized interface for interacting with the graph database, allowing agents such as the CodeGraphAgent to construct a knowledge graph of code entities using Memgraph and Tree-sitter AST parsing. The use of a graph database enables efficient querying and traversal of the code entities, facilitating the generation of insights and the detection of relationships between entities.

[LLM] The SemanticAnalysisAgent, implemented in the file integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/semantic-analysis-agent.ts, performs comprehensive semantic analysis of code files and git history. This agent utilizes the Tree-sitter AST parsing library to analyze the code structure and extract relevant information, such as function calls, variable declarations, and control flow. The agent also integrates with the OntologyClassificationAgent to classify the extracted information against the ontology system, enabling the component to generate insights and detect patterns in the codebase.

[LLM] The component implements work-stealing concurrency via a shared atomic index counter in the runWithConcurrency function, allowing multiple agents to execute concurrently and improving the overall performance of the component. This concurrency mechanism is essential for handling large-scale codebases, as it enables the component to process multiple files and entities simultaneously, reducing the overall processing time. The use of a shared atomic index counter ensures that the agents can safely access and update the index, preventing conflicts and ensuring correct execution.

[LLM] The ContentValidationAgent, implemented in the file integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/src/agents/content-validation-agent.ts, is responsible for validating entity content and detecting staleness in observations and insights. This agent checks the entity content against a set of predefined rules and constraints, ensuring that the content is consistent and up-to-date. The agent also integrates with the SemanticAnalysisAgent to detect staleness in observations and insights, enabling the component to update and refresh the knowledge graph as necessary. The use of a content validation agent ensures that the component provides accurate and reliable insights, and helps to maintain the integrity of the knowledge graph.

The SemanticAnalysis component is a multi-agent pipeline located under `integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/` that processes git history, LSL (Live Session Log) sessions, and AST-parsed code graphs to extract and persist structured knowledge entities. It orchestrates several specialized agents — GitHistoryAgent, VibeHistoryAgent, CodeGraphAgent, SemanticAnalysisAgent, OntologyClassificationAgent, ContentValidationAgent, and PersistenceAgent — each responsible for a discrete analytical concern, with a shared `BaseAgent<TInput, TOutput>` abstract class providing a standard response envelope, confidence scoring, issue detection, and routing suggestion framework.

BaseAgent<TInput, TOutput> (src/agents/base-agent.ts) enforces a uniform execute() → process() → calculateConfidence() → detectIssues() → generateRouting() → applyCorrections() lifecycle, ensuring every agent emits a typed AgentResponse envelope with metadata, routing hints, and corrections regardless of internal implementation.

SemanticAnalysisAgent (src/agents/semantic-analysis-agent.ts) writes optional trace JSON files to a `logs/` directory (e.g., `semantic-analysis-trace-<timestamp>.json`) on every analyzeGitAndVibeData() call, capturing full input payloads for ultra-debug purposes while explicitly treating write failures as non-fatal to avoid aborting the pipeline.

CodeGraphAgent (src/agents/code-graph-agent.ts) uses a TCP socket probe via net.Socket with a configurable timeout from loadAgentTuningConfig().code_graph.memgraph_check_timeout_ms to determine Memgraph reachability before attempting Tree-sitter indexing, and gracefully sets skipped=true on the CodeGraphAnalysisResult when the CLI or graph DB is unavailable.

OntologyClassificationAgent (src/agents/ontology-classification-agent.ts) uses a singleton OntologyConfigManager with a resetInstance() fallback to support test isolation, and chains OntologyManager → OntologyValidator → OntologyClassifier with a heuristic classifier created via createHeuristicClassifier() from src/ontology/heuristics/index.js for pre-LLM classification.

ClassificationProcessResult in ontology-classification-agent.ts aggregates per-classification llmUsage (model, provider, prompt/completion tokens) and rolls them up into a summary.llmUsage object tracking totalTokens, modelsUsed, and providersUsed, enabling cost attribution across the entire batch.

ContentValidationAgent (src/agents/content-validation-agent.ts) caches git commits in memory with a 60-second TTL (GIT_CACHE_TTL_MS = 60000) to prevent redundant git fetches during batch entity validation, and delegates git-based staleness detection to a dedicated GitStalenessDetector collaborator class.

SemanticAnalysisAgent enriches codeAnalysis.architecturalPatterns post-LLM by merging LLM-identified patterns from semanticInsights.keyPatterns into the heuristic-detected set, deduplicating by lowercased name, and defaulting confidence to 0.7 for LLM-sourced patterns that lack explicit scoring.

The SemanticAnalysis component is an MCP server-based multi-agent pipeline (`integrations/mcp-server-semantic-analysis/`) that processes git history and LSL (Live Session Log) sessions to extract, classify, validate, and persist structured knowledge entities. It orchestrates specialized agents—GitHistoryAgent, VibeHistoryAgent, CodeGraphAgent, SemanticAnalysisAgent, OntologyClassificationAgent, ContentValidationAgent, PersistenceAgent, and InsightGenerationAgent—each handling a distinct phase of analysis. The pipeline can be triggered via MCP tools (execute_workflow) or run incrementally on changed files.

Architecturally, all agents inherit from `BaseAgent<TInput, TOutput>` (base-agent.ts), which enforces a standard response envelope pattern including confidence scoring, issue detection, routing suggestions, and corrections. Agents use lazy LLM initialization via `ensureLLMInitialized()` backed by `@rapid/llm-proxy`'s `LLMService`, enabling provider-agnostic AI calls. The pipeline supports configurable analysis depths ('surface', 'deep', 'comprehensive') and integrates AST-based code graph data from a Memgraph-backed `code-graph-rag` MCP server via `CodeGraphAgent`.

Key cross-cutting patterns include ontology-driven classification (upper/lower ontology JSON files under `.data/ontologies/`), git-based staleness detection for validating persisted observations against recent commits, and GraphDatabaseAdapter-backed persistence with automatic JSON export sync. The system also tracks LLM token usage aggregated per classification batch and supports heuristic, LLM, and hybrid classification methods.

All agents extend `BaseAgent<TInput, TOutput>` (agents/base-agent.ts), which wraps every `process()` call in a standard response envelope via `createAgentResponse()`, automatically computing confidence breakdowns, detecting issues, generating routing suggestions, and handling errors uniformly.

`OntologyClassificationAgent` (agents/ontology-classification-agent.ts) uses a singleton `OntologyConfigManager` with upper (`development-knowledge-ontology.json`) and team-specific lower ontology files from `.data/ontologies/`, supporting 'heuristic', 'llm', 'hybrid', and 'auto-assigned' classification methods with per-classification LLM token budgets (default 500 tokens).

`CodeGraphAgent` (agents/code-graph-agent.ts) integrates with an external `code-graph-rag` MCP server by spawning `uv` CLI subprocesses and connecting to Memgraph via TCP (default port 7687); it gracefully skips indexing and sets `skipped: true` on the result if either `uv` or Memgraph is unavailable, preventing pipeline failure.

`SemanticAnalysisAgent.analyzeGitAndVibeData()` (agents/semantic-analysis-agent.ts) writes debug trace JSON to `logs/semantic-analysis-trace-<timestamp>.json` at pipeline entry as a non-fatal diagnostic, then branches analysis depth: 'surface' reads max 5 files and skips cross-analysis, while 'deep'/'comprehensive' performs full file reading and LLM-driven cross-correlation.

`ContentValidationAgent` (agents/content-validation-agent.ts) extracts file paths, commands, component class names (matching `*Agent`, `*Service`, `*Manager`, `*Adapter` patterns), and API endpoints from stored observation text using regex pattern arrays, then verifies their existence in the live codebase to produce per-entity `EntityValidationReport` with a 0–100 score.

`ContentValidationAgent` caches git commits for up to 60 seconds (`GIT_CACHE_TTL_MS = 60000`) to avoid redundant git fetches during batch entity validation, and delegates commit-to-entity correlation to a dedicated `GitStalenessDetector` (agents/git-staleness-detector.ts).

`ClassificationProcessResult` (agents/ontology-classification-agent.ts) aggregates LLM usage statistics across all classifications in a batch—total prompt/completion tokens, models used, providers used—enabling cost tracking and reporting at the workflow level.

attributes.name: LLMAbstraction
attributes.description:
[LLM] The LLMAbstraction component uses a provider-agnostic approach, allowing for easy switching between different LLM providers. This is achieved through the ProviderRegistry class (lib/llm/provider-registry.js), which manages the different LLM providers and their configurations. For instance, the AnthropicProvider class (lib/llm/providers/anthropic-provider.ts) is used to interact with the Anthropic API, while the DMRProvider class (lib/llm/providers/dmr-provider.ts) is used for local LLM inference.
